To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) children’s acquisition of inflection is sensitive to surface frequency, phonological neighbourhood density, case variance, affixedness and syncretism; (b) these effects are similar across the three languages; (c) children’s performance is more consistent with analogy-based than rule-based theories of inflectional learning.

the acquisition of inflected forms is affected by surface-form frequency, phonological neighbourhood density, and the number of cases a form is used in, and these effects are similar for the languages studied.

the acquisition of inflecting languages involves a combination of rule-like and analogy-like processes.

the results of the present study are most compatible with a hybrid model that combines rule-based and analogy-based approaches.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the acquisition of inflections is a complex phenomenon, and the findings of the present study are best interpreted as a result of a complex interplay between the language-specific properties of inflections and the general properties of the language-learning mechanism.
children's acquisition of inflection in Polish, Finnish and/or Estonian can be better explained by analogy-based accounts.

children's early morphological development is best understood as the gradual development of a connectionist network, in which the most frequent and salient exemplars are stored in memory and retrieved directly from memory, while the less frequent exemplars are retrieved via analogy to the stored exemplars, with the strength of analogy being a function of both frequency and similarity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the acquisition of inflections can be studied using the same methods and analyses that are applied to the acquisition of other aspects of language.
the acquisition of inflected forms is a gradual process, with children using both analogy and rule-based processes, and that the relative importance of these two processes is language-specific.

the acquisition of inflecting morphology is not a unitary phenomenon, and that it is necessary to take a cross-linguistically-informed approach that considers both language-general and language-specific properties of inflection.
